title: Leflunomide for Arthritis: Blood Tests and Warning Signs
meta_title: Leflunomide: Blood Tests, Side Effects and Pregnancy
meta_description: Taking leflunomide for arthritis? Understand blood tests, serious rash and infection warnings, pregnancy precautions and why stopping may need a washout.
excerpt: A practical guide to leflunomide monitoring and warning signs, with clear pregnancy advice and an honest explanation of conflicting paternal-exposure guidance.
direct_answer: Leflunomide is a daily DMARD for inflammatory arthritis. Benefit builds over weeks to months. Follow your blood-test and blood-pressure plan. Rash, mouth ulcers, fever, bruising, jaundice or breathing problems need urgent advice. Do not take it if pregnant or pregnancy is suspected; seek specialist help immediately. Its effects can persist after stopping.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: leflunomide, leflunomide blood tests, leflunomide side effects, leflunomide rash, leflunomide pregnancy, leflunomide washout

citations.label: NHS shortness of breath emergency advice

content:
Quick answer: Leflunomide is a DMARD for inflammatory arthritis, not an instant painkiller. Benefit builds over weeks to months, and blood tests plus blood-pressure checks are part of treatment. A new rash, mouth ulcers, fever, bruising, jaundice or breathing problem needs urgent advice. The medicine can remain in the body long after stopping, so serious reactions, switching treatment and pregnancy need a specialist plan.

First check: warning symptoms and urgent help

This guide is for adults prescribed leflunomide for rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis. It does not diagnose side effects or provide a dose or washout prescription. Do not assume a new symptom is harmless because it appears in a list of common effects.

  • Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty or a serious allergic reaction. Warning signs include gasping, being unable to get words out, a tight throat, sudden swelling of the lips or tongue, or collapse. Do not drive yourself to A&E.
  • A severe spreading, blistering or peeling rash needs emergency assessment now. A painful rash with mouth, eye or genital sores, especially after starting a medicine, can be a serious skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Follow NHS advice to call 999 or go to A&E; do not drive yourself. Take your medicines with you.
  • For a new skin rash or mouth ulcers, stop taking leflunomide and contact a doctor immediately. The patient information leaflet gives this instruction because these can signal a serious reaction. Do not simply wait for the next routine appointment or treat a rash yourself while continuing treatment.
  • Get urgent medical advice immediately for fever or sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked pallor or weakness, yellow eyes or skin, abdominal pain with feeling ill, new cough or breathlessness, or new tingling, weakness or pain in the hands or feet. These can indicate infection or problems affecting blood cells, liver, lungs or nerves.

Contact your GP or rheumatology urgent-advice service without delay. If your team is unavailable, use the local urgent-care route; NHS 111 is an option in England, Scotland and Wales. In Northern Ireland use your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Use 999 for an emergency. A recent normal blood test does not rule out a new serious problem. Ask urgently what to do about the next dose when a serious reaction or infection is suspected.

If you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant, do not take leflunomide and contact your specialist immediately. This is a specific exception to routine advice not to change arthritis treatment yourself. Stopping tablets alone may not remove the medicine quickly enough. The pregnancy section below explains why urgent specialist care matters.

What benefit to expect, and when

Leflunomide is a conventional disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug, or DMARD. It reduces the overactive immune response involved in inflammatory arthritis and can reduce joint pain, swelling and stiffness over time. It is not an extra painkiller to take when a joint hurts, and it is not a general treatment for osteoarthritis.

Arthritis UK describes an initial effect after about four to six weeks, with full benefit sometimes taking four to six months. The patient leaflet also says improvement can continue over that longer period. This is not a promise that everyone improves or a reason to ignore worsening symptoms. Agree a review date and a plan for pain and swelling while waiting.

Keep taking routine treatment as prescribed unless your team advises otherwise, but do not let that general advice override the urgent rash, allergy or pregnancy instructions above. If treatment is not helping enough, your team can review the plan rather than you adding tablets or making an unplanned switch.

Make the daily prescription unambiguous

Leflunomide is usually taken once daily. Follow your own label and rheumatology instructions; this article does not set a starting or loading dose. If you also take weekly methotrexate, keep its separate weekly schedule clear. These medicines do not have interchangeable dosing instructions.

Swallow leflunomide tablets whole with water, with or without food. Taking it at the same time each day can help you remember. If you miss a dose, the leaflet advises taking it when remembered unless the next dose is nearly due. Do not double the dose to catch up. Ask a pharmacist if unsure about timing or vomiting after a dose.

If you take more than prescribed, contact a doctor or get medical advice promptly, even if you are not sure whether symptoms are related. Keep the packet available. Do not wait for yellow skin, bleeding or another warning symptom to prove that you took too much.

Blood tests, blood pressure and follow-through

Leflunomide can affect the liver and blood cells and can raise blood pressure. Monitoring can include full blood count, liver and kidney function, blood pressure and weight. Before treatment, your team also checks suitability, infection risks and vaccination history. Tell them about existing liver, lung, kidney or nerve problems and previous medicine reactions.

Checks are usually closer together when treatment starts or changes, but the timetable must come from your own team. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service monitoring page says it is being updated for newer British Society for Rheumatology guidance. Published schedules differ, so this guide does not replace your shared-care plan with a universal calendar.

Ask who books each test, who checks the result and who will contact you. Record the next date and what to do if a test is missed. If methotrexate is prescribed alongside leflunomide, ask about the extra monitoring this combination may need. Do not stop either medicine simply because you have read that an interaction is possible, but do not add or restart a DMARD without specialist advice.

Diarrhoea, nausea and other effects still deserve a review

Diarrhoea, nausea, headache, dizziness, hair thinning or weight change can occur. Report troublesome effects rather than assuming you must tolerate them for months. Persistent diarrhoea needs assessment, particularly with weight loss, abdominal pain, blood in the stool, dehydration or feeling unwell. New rash, mouth ulcers or nerve symptoms belong in the urgent advice section, even though they can appear in common-effect lists.

Ask your pharmacist before adding a diarrhoea treatment or another shop-bought remedy. If vomiting or diarrhoea makes drinking difficult, seek advice; fluid advice may need to be different if you have a prescribed restriction. If dizzy, do not drive or operate machinery. A change in dose or medicine is a prescribing decision, not a home experiment.

Why stopping does not always end exposure

Leflunomide's active substance can persist for a long time, potentially up to two years without an accelerated removal procedure. This matters after a serious reaction, before some treatment changes and when planning pregnancy. Tell any new prescriber about previous leflunomide use, not only the tablets you currently take.

A specialist may arrange a washout using a prescribed medicine such as cholestyramine or activated charcoal. This is not a detox supplement or an over-the-counter charcoal routine. The medicine, course, testing and follow-up must be arranged by the clinical team. Do not assume that finishing a course, waiting a set number of days or stopping tablets means it is safe to conceive or start another medicine.

Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fathering a child

Leflunomide should not be taken during pregnancy or when pregnancy is suspected. Use effective contraception and speak to your rheumatology team well before trying to become pregnant. They can plan an alternative arthritis treatment, washout where needed and confirmation of when contraception can stop. Do not use a calendar calculation from this article as clearance to try for a baby.

If pregnancy occurs during treatment, British Society for Rheumatology guidance recommends stopping immediately and arranging a washout, with specialist pregnancy assessment considered. Contact the team urgently, do not wait for a routine review. Exposure does not prove that a baby has been harmed; the next step is prompt individual advice. Tell the team about previous leflunomide use even after stopping. Leflunomide is not recommended while breastfeeding.

Advice for men is different, and published sources disagree. The BSR pregnancy guideline considers paternal exposure compatible with pregnancy, and NRAS reflects that advice. However, the BNF and product leaflet retain contraception and possible washout precautions for men. Do not assume that every man must stop, or that an existing contraception plan can be ignored. Ask your specialist to reconcile the guidance for your circumstances before changing treatment or contraception.

Alcohol, infection, vaccines and other medicines

The product leaflet and NRAS advise avoiding alcohol because of liver toxicity. Arthritis UK gives more permissive limits for some patients. This guide does not turn that difference into a personal safe allowance: check your own team and leaflet, and do not treat a national drinking limit as permission to drink on leflunomide.

Tell your team promptly about contact with chickenpox or shingles, or if you develop either illness; treatment may be needed. Tell vaccination services that you take leflunomide. Live vaccines are generally avoided and the medicine's persistence matters after stopping too, so let the team set the timing. This article does not give current vaccine eligibility rules.

Ask for a full medicine check before new prescriptions, herbal products or shop-bought remedies. Warfarin and other blood thinners, some statins and other immune-modifying medicines can need particular attention. This is not a complete interaction list. Carry an up-to-date medicine list and ask about an immunosuppressive therapy alert card. Tell surgical and dental teams about current and recent treatment; do not decide on a pre-operation pause yourself.

A short plan to take away

  • My dose instructions, next blood-test date and blood-pressure check are recorded.
  • I know who checks results and whom to call urgently about rash, infection or the next dose.
  • My team knows about other medicines, alcohol, planned procedures and pregnancy or fertility plans.
  • I understand that stopping leflunomide does not automatically remove it from my body.

General UK educational information, not an individual treatment plan. Living With Arthritis is independent of Arthritis UK. A fresh qualified clinical review of this revision is pending.

key_takeaways: Keep your own blood-test and blood-pressure plan; full benefit can take several months.
A new rash or mouth ulcers requires stopping leflunomide and immediate advice. Severe blistering rash or breathing difficulty needs emergency care.
Pregnancy and suspected pregnancy need urgent specialist advice. Stopping tablets does not automatically clear leflunomide from the body.
